story_vision: Fixed author brief for a 30-Book epic fantasy Series. Experience: wonder, discovery, meaningful adventure, everyday belonging, emotionally consequential relationships and an ultimately hopeful possibility of flourishing. The Series must transform its civilization, institutions, relationships and narrative concerns across generations. Major victories change the world rather than restore the initial situation. Some conflicts emerge from consequences of earlier successes. Several characters, communities or institutions have independent agency. The Series permits local closure plus continuing long-range questions, and must not depend on escalating antagonists, arbitrary new threats or indefinitely postponed revelations. Use a fresh original Series concept; do not reuse the prior Wandering Islands answers, Book 11 prose or crossing mechanism. Scope of this exercise: an abstract whole-Series architecture only, not manuscripts or per-Book outlines.

architecture.summary: The Spring Ledger (working, noncanonical): a terraced highland valley is watered from a glacier-fed spring. Water reaches the terraces only where its shares are recorded, and each share creates a labour return owed to the channels. Three co-governing engines interact: the Ledger (recorded shares and owed returns), the Source (the spring's physical balance, which rises or falls with the gap between draw and return and is not a character), and the Old Hand (the interpretive legitimacy that decides whether a return is a debt, a gift or a contract). The series' central question is who gives back the water and whether giving must be counted. Governing role rotates across five macro arcs (Reckoned Water, Books 1-5; The Turn, 6-11; The Old Hand, 12-18; Settled Water, 19-22; Unmeasured, 23-30). Each arc ends in a changed governing engine, and each victory changes institutions (Stone Hall, Terrace Council, Mill Compact, Reading Hall) that act from their own agency. Renewal comes from feasibility, distribution and legitimacy pressures generated by earlier outcomes, not from escalating antagonists. Nothing here is accepted Identity, Structure or Book canon; the fixed author brief is the only fixed input.

nodes.title: Central question
nodes.summary: Who gives back the water, and must giving be counted? The question changes meaning as the Old Hand readings change what a return is.

nodes.title: Custody of the record
nodes.summary: Who holds the Ledger and on whose authority. Custody is the Stone Hall's source of legitimacy until Book 5 and contested afterwards.

nodes.title: Keeping the channels
nodes.summary: Who performs the return labour that keeps the spring balanced, and at what cost to families with few hands.

nodes.title: Reading the First Stones
nodes.summary: Who may read the oldest script and which reading becomes binding. Partial readings are scheduled in Books 1, 8 and 12; the full reading is Book 15.

nodes.title: Ledger engine
nodes.summary: Recorded shares set the draw. Credit can be falsified or favoured (Book 1), opened (Book 5), traded (Book 6), and re-read as gift or contract (Book 15). Each change alters who must return labour.

nodes.title: Source engine (physical commons)
nodes.summary: The spring's balance follows the gap between draw and return. Thinning leaves channels dry and floods wild water below; surfeit brings stagnant pools and fever. It responds to balance rather than to any character's intention, and it constrains which recorded shares can honestly be honoured.

nodes.title: Old Hand engine (interpretive legitimacy)
nodes.summary: Readings of the First Stones change what a share is: debt (Stone Hall), gift (Terrace Council) or contract (Mill Compact). A reading changes whether returns are recorded and therefore the balance on the Source.

nodes.title: The seasonal turn
nodes.summary: The rhythm of return labour across the terraces, repeated each season with changing participants. It makes belonging visible and provides the recurring scene texture across Books.

nodes.title: Wonder at a responsive order
nodes.summary: The reader's sense that the valley's order is larger and more responsive than any institution assumed.

nodes.title: Everyday belonging
nodes.summary: The warmth of shared labour and meals, which the series must keep specific across generations.

nodes.title: Consequential loss
nodes.summary: Grief and anger that follow from changed standing: those once credited lose standing, and those once uncounted gain it.

nodes.title: Hopeful flourishing
nodes.summary: The earned sense that a shared practice can outlast the institution that began it. The finale must show the cost.

nodes.title: Stone Hall (Reckoners)
nodes.summary: Hereditary keepers of the Ledger. Acts from its own agency: dissolves in Book 5 but a remnant under Keeper Corrow continues as a dissenting institution (typed as other because v2 has no institution category).

nodes.title: Terrace Council
nodes.summary: Formed in Book 6 from families who take the Turn. Holds maintenance decisions and argues for gift-return. Acts from its own agency.

nodes.title: Mill Compact
nodes.summary: Lowland grain-buyers who purchase shares once records open. Pursues contract-debt and trade interests from outside the valley. Acts from its own agency.

nodes.title: Reading Hall
nodes.summary: Founded after the full reading in Book 15 to make the First Stones publicly readable. Its rival readings sustain the Old Hand engine.

nodes.title: Epic fantasy
nodes.summary: Governing genre: the quest is to understand a physical commons that answers choices, not to defeat a rival power.

nodes.title: Pastoral belonging
nodes.summary: Supporting genre: belonging produced by shared return labour and eroded by unshared draw.

nodes.title: Political-institutional
nodes.summary: Supporting genre: institutions compete for legitimacy over custody and distribution of the record. Governs Arc 2 at phase level.

nodes.title: Mystery and discovery
nodes.summary: Tertiary genre: partial knowledge of the record and the spring changes choices; readings are staged so discovery advances by Book.

phases.title: Reckoned Water

trope_functions: the field that does not match the record
genre_activations.structural_function: a lower-terrace household discovers falsified credit and the Stone Hall's sealed custody is exposed (Book 1); the public record breaks the monopoly (Book 5).

phases.reader_experience: wonder at the first hidden chamber under the spring; anger at falsified credit
phases.narrative_function: The Ledger governs. Stone Hall credit is proven false; a lower terrace runs wild; the Hall's monopoly breaks at a local cost. Book 1 gives the first partial reading of the First Stones. Protagonist's agency comes from evidence and a coalition, not inheritance.
phases.transition: Records open, so shares become tradable and the spring shows its first recorded thinning.

phases.title: The Turn

trope_functions: the compromise that feeds a new market
genre_activations.structural_function: lowland Mill Compact purchases shares from freed households; draw separates from return; the upper cistern thins (Book 6). The Turn is sworn and the Terrace Council forms (Books 7-11).

phases.reader_experience: belonging tested by sale; anger at a market in shares
phases.narrative_function: The Source governs. Open records make shares a commodity. The Compact's purchases draw water without return labour, so the physical balance is the constraint that decides what the institutions can do. Partial reading of the First Stones (Book 8) makes the Old Hand contested knowledge.
phases.transition: Maintenance becomes an institution (the Turn) and the Old Hand becomes disputed knowledge.

phases.title: The Old Hand

trope_functions: the reading that reframes an earlier debt
genre_activations.structural_function: the complete reading of the First Stones (Book 15) makes the first compact a gift-return; the Stone Hall remnant holds it as debt, the Council as gift, the Compact as contract. An Unmeasured Return is tried in Lower Ammen and causes surfeit in the high terraces, forcing a new stewardship tally.

phases.reader_experience: wonder that the first compact was not a debt; fear of the surfeit
phases.narrative_function: The Old Hand governs. Legitimacy no longer rests on the Ledger alone. The Unmeasured Return is a costly, physically consequential choice: it stabilises the lower valley and disturbs the high cistern. The Reading Hall is founded as a public institution with its own readings.
phases.transition: Legitimacy is contested among three readings; no single institution holds the record.

phases.title: Settled Water

genre_activations.structural_function: terraces adopt different practices (Turn, stewardship tally, unmeasured return); plurality is tested for the first time; small local disputes arise from settled practice rather than from new antagonists.

phases.reader_experience: warmth of ordinary plurality; the bittersweet loss of single custody
phases.narrative_function: Co-governance. Ledger, Source and Old Hand share the field and no single engine dominates. This arc is deliberately lighter; its conflicts must come from settled practice, and it is the most likely place for filler.
phases.transition: Practice passes to the next generation.

phases.title: Unmeasured

trope_functions: the hidden order answers the people who keep it
genre_activations.structural_function: the generation raised under open accounts and unmeasured return overdraws the upper cistern for the Brightwater festival (Book 23); in Book 30 the spring's deepest cycle meets a choice between restored monopoly and shared accounting of care, which accepts a visible cost.

phases.reader_experience: hope that is earned by cost; wonder at the deepest chamber
phases.narrative_function: The Source is the physical crisis-maker, but its crisis is caused by earlier successes (abundance without memory). The finale chooses shared accounting that informs rather than binds, and accepts that some lowland and lower-terrace families must rebuild channels with their neighbours.
phases.transition: Series closes locally; a shared practice and long-range questions continue.

open_questions: Does the spring respond to intent, or only to measured balance? Book 15 gives a partial answer; the full ontology is deliberately not promised.
What do the lowland towns owe Ammen, and what does Ammen owe them?
Will any terrace keep a measured ledger in Book 30, and is plurality of practice the intended end state?
Who carries the Turn when the maintenance lineages end?
How many Brightwater shares may be drawn before the Balance Stones restrain them?
Is the Book 30 flood survived without losses or with lasting ones? This is an author choice and is not decided.

concepts.definition: A recurring abstract idea or concept explored throughout the narrative. Themes are not concrete entities but intellectual or emotional explorations.
concepts.name: Theme

concepts.definition: Opposition or challenge involving at least two forces with incompatible goals. Conflict creates narrative tension and drives progression.
concepts.name: Conflict

concepts.definition: A progression over time from a starting state to an ending state. Arcs can track character development, story progression, or thematic exploration.
concepts.name: Arc

relationships.description: Arc contains one or more beats
Arc involves one or more characters
Arc explores one or more themes
Arc contains one or more conflicts

concepts.definition: The introduction of an element, promise, or mystery that requires later resolution. Setups create expectations that drive narrative forward.
concepts.name: Setup

concepts.definition: The resolution or delivery of something set up earlier in the narrative. Payoffs satisfy expectations created by setups.
concepts.name: Payoff

concepts.definition: The disclosure of information previously unknown to the audience or characters. Revelations change understanding and can reframe entire narratives.
concepts.name: Revelation

concepts.definition: An unexpected change that inverts the direction or expected outcome of an arc. Reversals violate established patterns and create surprise.
concepts.name: Reversal

concepts.definition: A desired outcome that an entity (typically a character) wants to achieve. Goals create motivation and can generate conflicts.
concepts.name: Goal

relationships.description: Goal is owned by a character

concepts.definition: A discrete, identifiable moment in the narrative. Beats are atomic narrative units that combine to form scenes and arcs.
concepts.name: Beat

concepts.definition: An object, image, or action that carries meaning beyond its literal interpretation. Symbols represent abstract concepts through concrete forms.
concepts.name: Symbol

concepts.definition: A connection between narrative entities (typically characters) that affects how they interact. Relationships have dynamics, stakes, and evolution.
concepts.name: Relationship

concepts.definition: An entity capable of agency within the narrative. Characters have identities, beliefs, goals, and can participate in relationships and arcs.
concepts.name: Character

relationships.description: Character pursues one or more goals
Character can appear in multiple arcs
Character engages in relationships with other entities

selection.not_story_intent: These shared ontology meanings constrain interpretation; they are not declarations of author preference or accepted canon.
selection.rationale: Foundational definitions and relationship directions are always included. Installed genre definitions are added only when explicitly named; an unnamed genre stays unknown.
